editorialDecl.p: Edgeworth’s spelling and punctuation are retained in transcription, including non-standard spelling, line breaks, and hyphenation of words. The long s and ligatured forms are silently emended.

div.p:
Mr. Chenevix who presents this letter must be
known to you by reputation - I beg leave to
introduce him to you - He knows several of
your friends in Paris - & I know him to be a
man of virtue and honour.

He will give you a pamphlet on the of
which we think highly - let us know your opinion
of it - I also send you a paper of Mr. Kirwan's
of which I say nothing - but hope that you will
say a great deal.

We were glad to see your hand once more
- Whether travelling or stationary your letters
are always instructive and entertaining
- beside the value which we annex to them
from the belief that they are meant as instances of kindness -

You mention Stewarts work with great de-
licacy & kindness - Mr. Stewart is a gentleman
to whom my family is under great obligations
- He was a father almost to one of my sons
who was a student at Edinburgh and a kind
friend to two more of my sons when they were
resident in that city - It is therefore with great
reluctance that I express any dissent to doc-
trines which he speaks of with so much partia-
lity in his last book - I cannot however perceive
distinctly in what he differs from those who assert
the existence of innate ideas: perhaps you can
show me the difference before I add some notes on
"Practical Education" to - I shall not mention his
name, but I must support the doctrine, which I
believe to be the best -

I am surprised, that with Mr. Stewarts system,
he did not advert to Gall, who says that he has
discovered that nerves from each of the several
organs of sense coalesce in particular parts of the
brain - & that they may be there distinguished -
I am told from good authority that Cuvier assents to
this - (Talk to Chenevix about it) - Now, though the
rest of Gall's system may be, and in my opinion
are absurd, yet all, that can be supported by facts,
should be attended to.

We are it is true, after all, as much at a loss to ac-
count for the perceptive faculty; but if Gall is right
we may conclude, that the brain is not an homo-
-geneous fluid substance, and that some of the
extraordinary hallucinations of intellect may
appear less mysterious than formerly -

As to materiality and immateriality I never
could comprehend how Religion was supported
by one belief or destroyed by the other - Mr. Tooke &
Mr. Stewart set out in exactly opposite directions
but, as they must argue in a circle they will neces
sarilynecessarily meet - and even, when they do, very little prac-
-ticalpractical utility can follow -

Not so my dear Sir from your admira
ble and useful book - yours I must call it for
without you it never would have been read &
consequently never could have been useful -
- We prize the work the more the more we study
it - Maria is beginning it a third time -
- There is a passage in your 3d. vol page 198 in
Italics which she thinks requires to be dilated &
explained - I understand what you mean, but
I wish that an exception should be there repeated
of certain crimes that do not admit of pecuniary
remuneration - murder - maiming - &c -

In Mr. Stewarts Essays on taste I admire
with you the aimiableamiable candor of the author
Indeed upon all occasions Mr. Stewart
shews a generous & kind disposition - I think
however, that most of what he says was familiar
to literary men before he wrote this last quarto -
and I fear that another quarto to illustrate &
follow out as the Scotch say the conclusions that
he wishes to draw will appear too much for the
subject.

We have long projected a short book
under the title of Popular Metaphysics - in which
we did not mean to combat seriatim the opinions
of Descartes, Locke, BerkelyBerkeley, Hume, Hartley & Stewart
but to shew what is known in useful metaphysics
& to point out the limits within which, were we
to write & talk forever our speculations must
be confined - use (consciousness of) what words we may the con-
nexion between our senses & our perceptions
must I fear forever remain a mystery - You would
write popular metaphysics infinitely better that we
could - will you? -

We wish exceedingly well to your Quakers but really
we have not time to contribute with our pens - Are there
subscribers to the work? if there are pray subscribe for Maria & me.
I hope, that your intended visit to this place will
not be frustrated by political bouleversement!
